This message comes from Thumbtack.
Avoiding your unfinished home projects
because you're not sure where to start?
Thumbtack knows homes so you don't have to.
Don't know the difference
between matte paint finish and satin,
or what that clunking sound from your dryer is?
With Thumbtack, you don't have to be a home pro,
you just have to hire one.
You can hire top-rated pros,

Download today.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump says he's going to start paying
for campaign-style ads himself,
instead of with taxpayer dollars,
as he's been doing in recent weeks.
In a post on Truth Social today,
Trump says the practice of using taxpayer money
for the ads is, quote, "a rather standard thing to do."
Legal experts say that is not the case.
Now Trump says he'll use money raised by MAGA Inc.,
a super PAC supporting himself and Republican candidates.
Iran says it has received a U.S. proposal
to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
There was no immediate comment from the U.S.,
as NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchi reports.
Iran's Speaker of Parliament and lead negotiator,
Mahmoud Khalibaf, said Iran received a U.S. proposal
via mediators, but did not provide any further details.
Khalibaf added that the U.S. had to agree
to the country's conditions before any deal would be made.
Last month, Iran had put forward an agreement
to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days
if the U.S. met its terms.
President Trump rejected the plan,
but said he was willing to continue talks.
Many of Iran's demands mirror those
in a June memorandum of understanding
that fell apart a month later.
They include easing of U.S. sanctions,
an end to a U.S. naval blockade,
and unfreezing of Iranian assets
in return for reopening the Strait.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
-The Supreme Court began a new term today.
The High Court heard a case over whether local governments
can sue oil and gas companies for climate change costs.
Boulder, Colorado officials argued that companies
like Suncor and Exxon should be accountable
for climate-related disasters.
The companies claim the Clean Air Act
gives the federal government regulatory power, not states.
There are only hours left for eligible voters to register
for next month's midterm elections
in some parts of the country,
as NPR's Hansilo Wong reports election officials
also recommend those already registered
to pay close attention to any further deadlines.
-Today is the last chance for eligible voters
to register or update their registration
in American Samoa, Arizona, Indiana, and Ohio,
plus many southern states,
include Arkansas, Florida, Georgia,
Kentucky, Mississippi, South Carolina, Tennessee,
and Texas.
And later this week, there are more voter registration
deadlines for the midterm elections.
Missouri closes registration this Wednesday.
Oklahoma's deadline is Friday,
and sign-ups in Delaware and Saturday.
If you're already registered, you can confirm your status
by visiting your state
or territory's official election website.
Election officials recommend checking before the deadline,
especially if you recently moved, changed your name,
or haven't voted in a while.
Hansilo Wong, NPR News.
-Former White House press secretary Caroline Levitt
is joining Fox News as a contributor.
At 29, she was the youngest person
to serve as press secretary.
She left the role at the end of August.
Levitt follows Kayleigh McEnany,
the former Trump press secretary who joined Fox in 2021.
Levitt said she looks forward to sharing her perspective
with Fox's audience.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Incumbent Brazilian President Luis Inacio Lula da Silva
will face senator and Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro
during a runoff election for the presidency.
Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro,
who's in prison for attempting a coup
after he lost the 2022 election.
The runoff election is on October 25th.
European diplomats say they are staying put in Kyiv.
That's despite the Russian government
saying over the weekend that people who stay
are putting themselves in danger as its attacks on the city
intensify, Terry Schultz reports.
-The European Union's ambassador to Ukraine,
Katerina Matronova, says all 25 EU countries
with ambassadors in Kyiv
are planning to maintain their presence despite the threat.
Matronova said the EU's own representatives are also staying.
In coordinated messages, many EU ambassadors
issued personal statements on social media as well,
saying they, quote, "take note with concern
of the Russian foreign ministry's threat
against diplomats and foreign citizens in Ukraine
and reminding Russia it is bound by international conventions
and laws not to attack civilians."
"We stay in Kyiv," is the final sentence
in the replicated texts.
Last year, the EU delegation building in Kyiv,
along with a residential block where many staff live,
were severely damaged by a Russian missile strike.
For "NPR News," I'm Terry Schultz in Brussels.
-Italian premier Giorgia Maloney has applied to trademark
her voice in a bid to bolster protections
against AI-generated deepfakes.
The application includes a short audio recording.
-I am Giorgia Maloney.
-That's "I am Giorgia Maloney."
Maloney has repeatedly warned about the dangers of deepfakes.
This is "NPR News" from Washington.
